dengue.q: How accurate are dengue rapid tests?
dengue.a: NS1 antigen tests are most sensitive in the first week; IgM/IgG serology is more reliable later. Combined NS1+IgM/IgG devices offer the best overall detection across the illness course. All rapid results are screening-grade and may need confirmation.

dengue.q: Can a dengue rapid test distinguish primary from secondary infection?
dengue.a: IgG/IgM patterns provide clues (IgM-dominant suggests primary; rapid IgG rise suggests secondary), but a rapid test alone cannot definitively classify — interpret with clinical and epidemiological context.

dengue.q: What is the diagnostic window for dengue NS1?
dengue.a: NS1 is typically detectable from day 1 of fever through the first week, before IgM reliably appears — making it the earliest viral antigen marker of acute dengue.

malaria.q: Which malaria rapid test should I stock?
malaria.a: A Pf/Pan (or Pf/Pv) combo — it detects P. falciparum (HRP2) and other species (pLDH) in one device, which matters because treatment differs by species.

malaria.q: How soon after fever does a malaria RDT turn positive?
malaria.a: RDTs detect antigen during active parasitemia, typically from symptom onset; very low parasite densities can give false negatives, so repeat testing may be needed.
Yes — HRP2 can remain detectable for weeks after treatment, so a positive Pf HRP2 result does not always indicate treatment failure.

hiv-std.q: What is the window period for an HIV rapid test?
hiv-std.a: Antibody tests typically become reactive 3–6 weeks after exposure (window period). A negative result inside the window does not rule out infection — repeat or confirm by antigen/antibody or molecular testing.

hiv-std.q: Can a syphilis rapid test tell active from past infection?
hiv-std.a: No — treponemal antibody tests stay positive after treatment. Distinguish active from past infection with a non-treponemal (RPR) titer.

hiv-std.q: Why do HIV and syphilis get screened together?
hiv-std.a: Both are bloodborne/STIs with overlapping risk groups and are standard in antenatal and blood-donor screening; combined devices reduce cost and steps.

hepatitis.q: Does a positive HCV antibody test mean active infection?
hepatitis.a: No — anti-HCV indicates exposure (current or past). Active infection requires confirmation with HCV RNA.

hepatitis.q: What is the earliest marker of hepatitis B?
hepatitis.a: HBsAg is the earliest viral antigen marker of acute HBV and a marker of chronic infection.

hepatitis.q: Can rapid tests distinguish acute from chronic hepatitis B?
hepatitis.a: No — HBsAg positivity alone cannot distinguish acute from chronic; this requires additional markers (IgM anti-HBc) and clinical context.

hpylori.q: Which H. pylori test is best for test-of-cure?
hpylori.a: Stool antigen (or urea breath test) — they detect active infection and can confirm eradication. Antibody tests stay positive after treatment and are unsuitable for test-of-cure.

hpylori.q: Do antibiotics or PPIs affect H. pylori stool antigen?
hpylori.a: Yes — recent PPI or antibiotic use can suppress detection and cause false negatives; testing is usually done after a washout period.
It indicates exposure but cannot distinguish active from past infection; use it mainly where stool testing or endoscopy is unavailable.

respiratory.q: How accurate are rapid flu/COVID/RSV antigen tests?
respiratory.a: Antigen tests are fast but less sensitive than molecular (PCR). A negative result during high prevalence does not exclude infection — confirm clinically or by PCR.

respiratory.q: When should I use a multiplex respiratory test?
respiratory.a: During respiratory season, when COVID, flu and RSV circulate together and symptoms overlap — a combo resolves the differential in one test.

respiratory.q: Do rapid antigen tests detect asymptomatic infection?
respiratory.a: Sensitivity is lower in asymptomatic or low-viral-load cases; antigen tests are most reliable in the early symptomatic phase.

cardiac.q: Can a rapid troponin test rule out a heart attack?
cardiac.a: A point-of-care qualitative troponin is a triage aid, not a replacement for high-sensitivity quantitative lab assays and serial testing.
D-dimer is used to help rule out venous thromboembolism (VTE) — a negative result is the clinical value; a positive result is non-specific.

cardiac.q: Which cardiac markers come in a panel?
cardiac.a: Common POC panels combine troponin I, CK-MB, myoglobin and sometimes D-dimer or H-FABP for early myocardial-injury assessment.

doa-workplace.q: What does a presumptive positive drug screen mean?
doa-workplace.a: A screening result that flags possible drug use; it must be confirmed by a definitive lab method (GC-MS/LC-MS) before any adverse action.

doa-workplace.q: What are adulteration checks in a drug test cup?
doa-workplace.a: Built-in strips for pH, specific gravity and oxidants that detect sample tampering at the point of collection.

doa-workplace.q: What cut-off levels should a workplace program use?
doa-workplace.a: Most align with SAMHSA-style cut-offs (e.g., THC 50 ng/mL, amphetamine/methamphetamine 500–1000 ng/mL, cocaine 150–300 ng/mL).

pregnancy-fertility.q: How early can a pregnancy test detect hCG?
pregnancy-fertility.a: Many tests detect hCG around the first day of a missed period (20–25 mIU/mL sensitivity); testing too early can give a false negative.

pregnancy-fertility.q: When is the best time to test for the LH surge?
pregnancy-fertility.a: Mid-cycle, testing daily in the afternoon/evening; the LH surge precedes ovulation by ~24–36 hours.

pregnancy-fertility.q: Can fFN or IGFBP-1 diagnose preterm labor?
pregnancy-fertility.a: No — they are risk-stratification aids used with clinical findings and gestational age, not standalone diagnostics.

tumor.q: Can a tumor marker rapid test diagnose cancer?
tumor.a: No — PSA, AFP and CEA rise in benign conditions too, and confirmation requires imaging and other testing. They are monitoring/screening-support aids.
Prostate cancer screening support and monitoring; elevated PSA prompts further evaluation (biopsy), but is not cancer-specific.
Hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) — used in high-risk surveillance and monitoring, alongside imaging.

tropical.q: Do dengue, Zika and chikungunya tests cross-react?
tropical.a: Yes — they are related viruses and serology can cross-react, so results must be interpreted with travel and epidemiological context.

tropical.q: Do tropical rapid tests need cold chain?
tropical.a: No — colloidal-gold lateral-flow tests are room-temperature stable, a key advantage for remote and tropical distribution.

tropical.q: What documentation do tender programs need?
tropical.a: CE/ISO certificates, validation data, COA, stability data and export documentation — request the full dossier before bidding.

gastrointestinal.q: Which viruses does a gastro rapid test panel cover?
gastrointestinal.a: Common panels detect rotavirus, adenovirus and norovirus — alone or in combination devices.
Fecal calprotectin distinguishes inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from functional disorders (IBS) — elevated levels indicate gut inflammation.

gastrointestinal.q: Is FOB testing useful for colorectal screening?
gastrointestinal.a: Yes — fecal occult blood testing is a first-line screening tool; a positive result requires colonoscopy follow-up.
